rv.q: Cicely Tyson and James Earl Jones bring decades of craft and chemistry to D.L. Coburn's Pulitzer Prize-winning play, making even its most familiar moments feel fresh and immediate.
These two superlative performers establish beyond doubt, if we needed any reminding, that great talent is ageless and ever-rewarding.
Watching them together is a sheer honor.
The partnership of Cicely Tyson and James Earl Jones comes very close.

James Earl Jones and Cicely Tyson bring commanding presence and lived-in authenticity to D.L. Coburn's Pulitzer Prize-winning play about two nursing home residents finding connection through card games.
They really are a match made in theater heaven.

"Under Leonard Foglia’s sensitive direction, the actors give their all to an almost-good play...Jones is more tentative here than usual, more halting in his speeches, more brittle than we expect Weller to be.
Light on tragedy and heavy on comedy—at least in this version—it’s an infallible vehicle for two aging stars who can lay on the charm.
Coburn’s view of human life is condescending and dyspeptic.
The age of the actors perhaps makes them slower and cuter than might be ideal; the result is likable but shambling.

Whether Jones and Tyson are having memorization problems I cannot say, but the production is so lame and misguided (by the director Leonard Foglia) you would almost prefer that they suddenly started ad libbing selections from far better work each of them has done. As it is, they stick at least to the outlines of the script.
It will add years to your life.
Leonard Foglia’s direction is as first rate as his cast.
Jones and Tyson are two of the theater's most valuable assets and to see them together on any stage is a rare treat not to be missed.
James Earl Jones is a marvel of hilarity spun out of sadness and loneliness and curmudgeonness and you ache for him, oh, gollies.
Along the way Jones and Tyson hold you, like the cards, in the palm of their hands.
James Earl Jones and Cicely Tyson are just as adept in mastering the rhythms of this play to keep us engaged.
What makes "...Gin Game" such a treat is watching these two consummate veterans deliver incredibly calibrated performances in what must be a very difficult play for actors of any age.
Jones and Tyson, it will surprise no one, make for lively sparring partners.
The great pleasure in the revival is watching the veteran performers work together with warmth and humor, not missing a beat.
If THE GIN GAME is a little thin on plot to fill out its two acts, it serves splendidly as a star vehicle for beloved senior actors.
Putting four-letter obscenities into the mouths of octogenarians -- okay, nonagenarian in Tyson's case -- is a cheap trick but it works.
What doesn’t work (except as an excuse to watch two pros go at it) is Coburn’s play, which won the Pulitzer Prize in 1978.
Their partnership onstage is comforting, if not necessarily elevating.
What should culminate in devastation — a vision of life's potential to leave us all alone and abandoned —is played instead as the vaudeville of a couple of eccentric codgers.
It’s Jones who anchors the show, especially gripping at depicting Weller as a broken man with a fierce temper who uses cards to try to numb the pain.
And no sooner does the scrim curtain rise on the cluttered, unused porch of the Bentley Old Folks residence than you know you're in fine hands.
Even if the rest of The Gin Game stalls, at delivering that essential theatrical element, Jones and Tyson are an unvarnished success.
Jones and Tyson are worth a better hand.
With two old pros holding court, “The Gin Game” is one of the best evenings in theater I’ve had in a long time.
Growing old in this world it seems, is no game at all.
Like it or not, that alone makes a visit worthwhile.
An enjoyable, diverting evening spent with two expert performers, nothing more, nothing less.
Both Jones and Tyson are terrific; yet the show never truly engaged me.
They are both superb and sublime.
It’s safe to say that there will not be a better performance than what Jones and Tyson present here.

cn.t: Critics praise the legendary performances of James Earl Jones and Cicely Tyson, whose chemistry and mastery elevate D.L. Coburn's slight, Pulitzer-winning play about nursing home residents into compelling theater, though most agree the material itself remains lightweight.

vs.sum: The John Golden Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, though sound quality can vary, especially under the mezzanine. Seating comfort is typical of older theaters with tight legroom, but the venue maintains a pleasant ambiance overall. Facilities are adequate, though not exceptional.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No wheelchair-accessible restroom (use adjacent Schoenfeld).
